purpose: Educational OSINT tool for learning deep/dark web concepts without accessing illicit content
legal_disclaimer: This tool uses only synthetic data and publicly documented concepts for educational purposes. It does not access the dark web or any illicit content.

modules.title: Surface vs Deep vs Dark Web

definitions.surface_web: Public websites indexed by search engines (Google, Bing). Examples: news sites, social media, e-commerce.
definitions.deep_web: Content not indexed by search engines. Includes email inboxes, paywalled content, private databases, internal portals. ~90%+ of internet.
definitions.dark_web: Hidden subset of deep web requiring special software (Tor). Uses .onion domains. Designed for anonymity. Hosts both legitimate privacy services and illicit markets.

key_differences: Surface web: indexed, public, standard browsers
Deep web: unindexed, private/auth-required, standard browsers
Dark web: hidden, anonymized, requires Tor/special protocols

quiz.question: Which layer of the web includes your email inbox?
quiz.explanation: Email inboxes are not indexed by search engines and require authentication, making them part of the deep web.

quiz.question: What software is required to access .onion domains?
quiz.explanation: .onion domains are only accessible through the Tor Browser or compatible Tor clients.

quiz.question: True or False: The dark web and deep web are the same thing.
quiz.explanation: They are different. The deep web is all unindexed content; the dark web is a small, anonymized subset requiring special software.

illicit_markets.description: Marketplaces selling stolen credentials, malware, phishing kits, exploits
illicit_markets.detection_relevance: Source of initial access tools, credential stuffing campaigns, phishing infrastructure

forums.description: Discussion boards for threat actors to share TTPs, tools, and coordinate
forums.detection_relevance: Early indicators of campaigns, tool development, vendor targeting

privacy_services.description: Legitimate anonymity tools, secure email, censorship-resistant hosting
privacy_services.detection_relevance: Understanding dual-use infrastructure; not all dark web activity is malicious

whistleblowing.description: Secure drop sites for journalists and activists
whistleblowing.detection_relevance: Legitimate use cases; important for threat intel context

mirrors.description: Censorship-resistant mirrors of surface-web services (news, social media)
mirrors.detection_relevance: Understanding onion service architecture; some are legitimate

quiz.question: Which dark-web service type is most relevant for early campaign indicators?
quiz.explanation: Forums often contain discussions about upcoming campaigns, tool development, and targeting strategies.

quiz.question: True or False: All dark-web services are illegal.
quiz.explanation: False. Many dark-web services are legitimate privacy tools, news mirrors, or whistleblowing platforms.

ttps.name: Credential Stuffing from Leaked Databases
ttps.description: Threat actors purchase leaked credentials from dark-web markets and automate login attempts across multiple services.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: High volume of failed logins from diverse IPs targeting same accounts; geographic anomalies in login attempts

synthetic_indicators.pattern: Multiple failed logins (>10) within 5 minutes from geographically dispersed IPs

ttps.name: Phishing Kit Distribution via Dark-Web Markets
ttps.description: Ready-to-deploy phishing kits (landing pages, credential harvesters, email templates) sold on dark-web marketplaces.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: Newly registered domains with lookalike branding; suspicious email attachments with credential harvesting forms

synthetic_indicators.pattern: Domains registered <7 days ago with typosquatting patterns targeting financial brands

ttps.name: Initial Access Brokering
ttps.description: Threat actors sell access to compromised corporate networks (via RDP, VPN, web shells) acquired through dark-web channels.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: Unusual RDP/VPN connections from unexpected geolocations; web shell artifacts on internet-facing servers

synthetic_indicators.log_example: 2026-10-02 03:22:05 VPN_CONNECT user=svc_backup src_ip=45.155.205.89 geo=NL time=03:22 local_time=22:22_prev_day
synthetic_indicators.pattern: Service account VPN connections from non-corporate IPs during off-hours

ttps.name: Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS)
ttps.description: Ransomware, info-stealers, and RATs offered via subscription or affiliate programs on dark-web forums.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: Known malware signatures; suspicious PowerShell/LOLBin usage; C2 beaconing patterns

synthetic_indicators.pattern: Encoded PowerShell commands spawned from office applications or browsers

detection_exercise.scenario: You observe the following log entries in your SIEM over a 2-hour window. Identify which TTP(s) might be occurring and write a detection rule.

detection_rule_template.name: Credential Stuffing Followed by Suspicious PowerShell
detection_rule_template.logic: ALERT IF (failed_logins > 10 within 5 minutes for same user) AND (success_login from same IP as failed attempts) AND (powershell.exe spawned from office app with encoded command)
detection_rule_template.false_positives: Legitimate penetration testing; password manager testing; user traveling internationally

scenario.title: Investigate a Dark-Web Mention in Threat Intel Report
scenario.background: Your threat intel team received a report mentioning a new phishing kit being sold on a dark-web marketplace. The report includes a synthetic .onion address and vendor name.

workflow_steps.guidance: Check if the threat intel vendor is reputable. Look for corroborating reports from other vendors.
Search for the vendor name and .onion address in public sources (news, blogs, forums).

modules.title: Your First Time on Tor: Safe Setup & Navigation

content.overview: Before you open a single .onion page, set up your environment and your rules. Most beginner mistakes (leaking your identity, getting phished, landing on something illegal) come from skipping this module. This content is guidance only: TGV-DarkINT itself never connects to Tor.

setup_options.name: Tor Browser (on a dedicated machine or profile)
setup_options.what: Official browser from torproject.org that routes traffic through the Tor network and standardises your fingerprint.
setup_options.good_for: Quick, low-risk reading of public onion sites.
setup_options.watch_out: Your host OS is still in the loop. Malware or a careless download can expose you. Only download it from torproject.org and keep it updated.

setup_options.name: Tails (live USB)
setup_options.what: Amnesic OS you boot from a USB stick. All traffic is forced through Tor and nothing is written to disk unless you enable encrypted Persistent Storage.
setup_options.good_for: Sensitive one-off sessions where you want zero local traces.
setup_options.watch_out: Everything is forgotten at shutdown, including your notes. Save notes to an encrypted USB. Tails ships its own Tor Browser.

setup_options.name: Whonix (two VMs)
setup_options.what: A Gateway VM that does the Tor routing plus a Workstation VM that can only reach the network through it. Even if the Workstation is compromised, it cannot learn your real IP.
setup_options.good_for: Analysts who need tools, snapshots and repeatable investigations. Runs on VirtualBox or KVM; Qubes-Whonix is the hardened option.
setup_options.watch_out: Heavier setup. Keep both VMs updated and revert to a clean snapshot after each session.

setup_options.name: VPN + Tor
setup_options.what: Connecting to a VPN first, then Tor ('Tor over VPN'), hides the fact that you use Tor from your ISP and local network.
setup_options.good_for: Environments where Tor use is flagged, or where company policy requires approved egress.
setup_options.watch_out: It is not magic anonymity. The VPN provider sees that you connect to Tor and you must trust their no-logs claim. Do not stack extra proxies without understanding the trade-off. Never use a VPN as a substitute for Tor Browser or Whonix.

do: Get authorization and write down your research objective first
Use a dedicated device, VM or Tails: no personal accounts, no personal files
Verify you are on Tor at check.torproject.org after launching
Set Tor Browser security level to Safer or Safest (Safest disables JavaScript)
Take notes and screenshots inside the VM, then store them encrypted
Defang indicators in your notes (hxxp://example[.]onion) so nobody clicks by accident
Revert the VM snapshot or shut down Tails after the session
dont: Log in to personal accounts or reuse usernames, emails or passwords
Maximize the browser window or install extensions (both make you more fingerprintable)
Torrent over Tor or download and open files while online
Buy anything, register on forums or chat with threat actors unless your role and legal team explicitly allow it
Trust any onion link you did not verify: scams and phishing clones are everywhere
Save, screenshot or share illegal content. Close it and report it

first_session.detail: Pick one option from the setup list (Tails or Whonix recommended for beginners), update it, and confirm no personal accounts are logged in.
Launch Tor Browser, let it connect, then open check.torproject.org to confirm you are using Tor. Set the security level to Safer or Safest.

Open DuckDuckGo (it works fine inside Tor Browser) and search for 'Ahmia search engine'. Ahmia is an open-source search engine for onion services that filters out abuse material. Open it from the official result and sanity-check the domain.

first_session.action: Search Ahmia for your research topic
first_session.detail: Use plain keywords tied to your objective (for example a leak site name or forum name from public threat reporting). Read result titles and snippets first. You do not have to open everything.

first_session.action: Find the maps: hidden wikis and onion directories
first_session.detail: Search Ahmia for 'hidden wiki' and 'onion directory' to learn how the ecosystem is organised. Treat every copy as unverified. Many are outdated, scam-run or link to illegal content, so browse them to understand the landscape, not to trust them.

first_session.action: Verify before you rely on a link
first_session.detail: Cross-check onion addresses against reputable public sources (vendor threat reports, official project pages, PGP-signed mirror lists). v3 onion addresses are 56 characters plus .onion. One wrong character means a different site.
Record what you saw with timestamps and defanged URLs, then close the session. Use 'New Identity' in Tor Browser, then power off Tails or revert the Whonix snapshot.

legal_ethics: Browsing is legal in most places, but laws differ. Know yours and your employer's policy before you start.
Never purchase, download malware, or interact with sellers. Observation only unless you are in an authorized, legally reviewed role.
If you stumble on child sexual abuse material, leave immediately, do not save or screenshot it, and report it to the IWF (iwf.org.uk), NCMEC (report.cybertip.org) or your local police.
Do not publish personal data you find about victims. Report it to the affected organization instead.

quiz.question: Which setup keeps your real IP hidden even if the machine you work in gets compromised?
options: Tor Browser on your everyday laptop
A browser extension that adds a proxy
quiz.explanation: In Whonix the Workstation can only reach the network through the Gateway, so malware inside it cannot discover your real IP.

quiz.question: What is the main trade-off of using a VPN before Tor?
options: It hides Tor use from your ISP but shifts trust to the VPN provider
quiz.explanation: Your ISP sees only VPN traffic, but the VPN provider can see that you connect to Tor. It is a trust trade-off, not a free upgrade.

quiz.question: You find a 'Hidden Wiki' page full of onion links. How should you treat it?
options: As unverified: great for learning the landscape, never for blind trust
Click every link to check them all
quiz.explanation: Hidden wiki copies are often outdated, scam-run or point to illegal content. Verify links against reputable public sources.

quiz.question: You accidentally land on illegal content involving children. What do you do?
options: Leave immediately, do not save anything, and report it
Keep browsing to see where it leads
quiz.explanation: Never save or share it. Close it and report to the IWF, NCMEC or local police.

final_quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a legitimate use case for the dark web?
final_quiz.explanation: Selling stolen credentials is illegal. Whistleblowing, news mirrors, and secure email are legitimate privacy-focused uses.

final_quiz.question: What is the primary detection hypothesis for credential stuffing attacks?
options: Single failed login from unusual location
Multiple failed logins from diverse IPs targeting same accounts
final_quiz.explanation: Credential stuffing involves automated login attempts from many IPs against the same accounts, resulting in high volumes of failed logins.

final_quiz.question: In the OSINT workflow, what is the first step after receiving dark-web threat intel?
options: Validate the source and check for corroboration
final_quiz.explanation: Always validate the source and look for corroborating reports before taking action or investing investigation time.

final_quiz.question: Which Tor Browser security level disables JavaScript?
final_quiz.explanation: Safest disables JavaScript on all sites. Safer disables it on non-HTTPS sites and some risky features.

final_quiz.question: Which of these should you NEVER do in a first Tor session?
options: Log in to a personal account
final_quiz.explanation: Logging in to a personal account ties the session to your real identity.
